# Introduction

Load packages:

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(package = tidyverse)
library(package = stringr)  # package for manipulating character data (part of tidyverse)
library(package = lubridate)  # package for working with dates and times
#library(package = rvest)  # package for reading and manipulating HTML; effectively destroyed when Musk bought Twitter!
```

-   Generic syntax: `install.packages(pkgs = "package_name")`
-   Install "tidyverse": `install.packages(pkgs = "tidyverse")`

**Note**: When we load package, name of package is not in quotes; but when we install package, name of package is in quotes:

-   `install.packages(pkgs = "tidyverse")`
-   `library(package = tidyverse)`

## Dataset we will use

We will use `rtweet` to pull Twitter data from the PAC-12 universities. We will use the university admissions Twitter handle if there is one, or the main Twitter handle for the university if there isn't one:

-   We wrote a short tutorial on using `rtweet` in the Fall 2020 version of this class:
    -   [LINK](https://anyone-can-cook.github.io/rclass1/in_class/rtweet/intro_to_rtweet.html) to html file
    -   [LINK](https://anyone-can-cook.github.io/rclass1/in_class/rtweet/intro_to_rtweet.Rmd) to .Rmd file

```{r}
# library(package = rtweet)

#          "engagestanford", "UtahAdmissions", "UW", "WSUPullman")

# p12_full_df <- readRDS(file = "p12_dataset.RDS")

p12_df <- p12_full_df %>% select("user_id", "created_at", "screen_name", "text", "location")

```

# Review of Data structures and types

What is an **object**?

-   Everything in R is an object
-   We can classify objects based on their **class** and **type**
    -   `class()`: What kind of object is it (high-level)?
        -   The class of the object determines what kind of functions we can apply to it
    -   `typeof()`: What is the object's data type (low-level)?
-   Objects may be combined to form **data structures**

[![](https://d33wubrfki0l68.cloudfront.net/1d1b4e1cf0dc5f6e80f621b0225354b0addb9578/6ee1c/diagrams/data-structures-overview.png){width="400px"}](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/vectors.html)

*Credit: [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/vectors.html)*

<br> Basic **data types**:

-   Logical (`TRUE`, `FALSE`)
-   Numeric (e.g., `5`, `2.5`)
-   Integer (e.g., `1L`, `4L`, where `L` tells R to store as `integer` type)
-   Character (e.g., `"R is fun"`)

Basic **data structures**:

_Review from Intro to R and Attributes and Class lectures:_ 

-   [Atomic vectors](https://anyone-can-cook.github.io/rclass1-redesign/lectures/updated_lectures/intro_to_r/intro_to_r.html#atomic-vectors)
-   [Lists](https://anyone-can-cook.github.io/rclass1-redesign/lectures/updated_lectures/intro_to_r/intro_to_r.html#lists)
    -   [Dataframes](https://anyone-can-cook.github.io/rclass1-redesign/lectures/updated_lectures/attributes_and_class/attributes_and_class.html#data-frames)



# Character data basics

What is **character data**?

-   `character` is a basic data type in R
-   Character values can contain letters, numbers, punctuation, and spaces
-   You can create character data using either single quotes (`'`) or double quotes (`"`)
    -   When R prints character data, it usually displays it with double quotes
-   The `class()` and `typeof()` of a character vector are both `character`
-   Informally, people often call one character value—a character vector with one element—a **string**.

<br> **Example**: Creating character data using single quotes

Notice how R displays the character value using double quotes:

```{r}
vec_x <- 'This is character data'
vec_x
```

<br> **Example**: Creating character data using double quotes

```{r}
vec_x <- "Character values can also contain numbers: 123"
vec_x
```

<br> **Example**: Checking the class and type of character data

```{r}
class(x = vec_x)
typeof(x = vec_x)
```

<br>
**Note: quotes have a special meaning in R: they mark the beginning and end of a character value.**

To include a quote as part of the text, you can:

- Surround the character value with the other type of quotes.
- Place a backslash (`\`) before the quote, which is called "escaping the single quote"
  - The backslash is the `escape character`
  - `\'` is an `escape sequence`
  - The backslash tells R to treat the quote as a literal character rather than as the end of the character value.

```{r}
# Use double quotes so the single quote is treated as ordinary text
vec_x <- "There's no issue with this example."
vec_x

# Use \' so the single quote is treated as ordinary text
vec_x <- 'There\'s no issue with this example.'
vec_x
```

```{r, eval=F}
# This would not work
vec_x <- 'There's an issue with this example.'
vec_x
```


*We won't be going in-depth into escaping characters for this class, but see appendix for more details if you are interested.*

- Understanding escape sequences is important for data science. [Rclass2](https://anyone-can-cook.github.io/rclass2/) covers this topic in greater detail in the lecture on [Strings and Regular Expressions](https://anyone-can-cook.github.io/rclass2/lectures/strings_and_regex/strings_and_regex.html)


<br>

# `stringr` package

> "A consistent, simple and easy to use set of wrappers around the fantastic `stringi` package. All function and argument names (and positions) are consistent, all functions deal with `NA`'s and zero length vectors in the same way, and the output from one function is easy to feed into the input of another."

*Credit: `stringr`[R documentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stringr/versions/1.4.0)*

The `stringr` package:

-   The `stringr` package is based off the `stringi` package and is part of **Tidyverse**
-   `stringr` contains functions for working with character data
-   For many functions in the `stringr` package, there are equivalent "base R" functions
-   But `stringr` functions all follow the same rules, while rules often differ across different base R character functions, so we will focus exclusively on `stringr` functions
-   Most `stringr` functions start with `str_` (e.g., `str_length`)

## `str_length()`

<br> **The `str_length()` function**:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
?str_length

# SYNTAX
str_length(string = vec_name)
```

-   Function: Find the number of characters in each element of a character vector
-   Arguments:
    -   `string`: Character vector (or vector coercible to character)
-   Note that `str_length()` counts the characters in each element, whereas `length()` counts the number of elements in an object

<br>


**Example**: Using `str_length()` on one character value

```{r}
str_length(string = "cats")
```

Compare to `length()`, which counts the character value as one element:

```{r}
length(x = "cats")
```


**Example**: Using `str_length()` on a character vector

```{r}
str_length(string = c("cats", "in", "hat"))
```

Compare to `length()`, which finds the number of elements in the vector:

```{r}
length(x = c("cats", "in", "hat"))
```


<details>

<summary>**Example**: Using `str_length()` on other vectors coercible to character</summary>

Logical vectors can be coerced to character vectors:

```{r}
str_length(string = c(TRUE, FALSE))
```

Numeric vectors can be coerced to character vectors:

```{r}
str_length(string = c(1, 2.5, 3000))
```

Integer vectors can be coerced to character vectors:

```{r}
str_length(string = c(2L, 100L))
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Using `str_length()` on dataframe column</summary>

Recall that the columns in a dataframe are just vectors, so we can use `str_length()` as long as the vector is coercible to character type. Let's look at the `screen_name` column from the `p12_df`:

```{r}
# `p12_df` is a dataframe object
str(object = p12_df)

# `screen_name` column is a character vector
str(object = p12_df$screen_name)
```

<br> **\[Base R method\]** Use `str_length()` to calculate the length of each `screen_name`:

```{r}
# Let's focus on just the unique screen names
unique(x = p12_df$screen_name)

str_length(string = unique(x = p12_df$screen_name))
```

<br> **\[Tidyverse method\]** Use `str_length()` to calculate the length of each `screen_name`:

```{r}
# Let's focus on just the unique screen names
p12_df %>% select(screen_name) %>% unique()

#p12_df %>% select(screen_name) %>% unique() %>% str_length()
```

Notice that the above line does not work as expected because we passed in a dataframe to `str_length()` and it is trying to coerce that to character:

```{r}
class(x = p12_df %>% select(screen_name) %>% unique())
```

An alternative way is to add a column to the dataframe that contains the result of applying `str_length()` to the `screen_name` vector:

```{r}
p12_df %>% select(screen_name) %>% unique() %>% 
  mutate(screen_name_len = str_length(string = screen_name))
```

</details>

## `str_c()`

```{r}
str_c(c("A", "B", "C"),c("a", "b", "c"))
```

<br> **The `str_c()` function**:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
?str_c

# SYNTAX AND DEFAULT VALUES
str_c(..., sep = "", collapse = NULL)
```

-   Function: Combine character vectors by joining their corresponding elements together
    -   Programmers sometimes say "concatenate" instead of "join"
-   Arguments:
    -   `...`: The input is one or more character vectors (or vectors coercible to character)
        -   Zero length arguments are removed
        -   One-element inputs are recycled to the common length of the input vectors
    -   `sep`: Character value to insert between corresponding elements from the input vectors
    -   `collapse`: Optional character value used to join the elements of the output vector into one element

````{=html}
<!--

str_c("a","b", sep = "", collapse = NULL)
str_c("a","b", sep = "~", collapse = NULL)

str_c("a","b", sep = "", collapse = ";")
str_c("a","b", sep = "~", collapse = ";")

str_c(c("a"),c("b"), sep = "~", collapse = ";")
str_c(c("a"),c("b"), sep = "", collapse = ";")
```

s1 <- c("s1e1","s1e2","s1e3")

str_c(s1, sep = "", collapse = NULL) %>% length()
str_c(s1, sep = "", collapse = NULL) %>% str_length()


str_c(s1, sep = "~", collapse = NULL)
str_c(s1, sep = "~", collapse = ";")

````

<br> **Example**: Using `str_c()` on one vector

Since we provided only one input vector, it has nothing to join element by element with, so `str_c()` returns the same vector:

```{r}
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"))
```

Note that specifying the `sep` argument will also not have any effect because we only have one input vector, and `sep` is the separator between multiple vectors:

```{r}
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"), sep = "~")

# Check length: Output is the original vector of 3 elements
str_c(c("a", "b", "c")) %>% length()
```

By default, `str_c()` returns a character vector containing the element-by-element results. The `collapse` argument joins those output elements together, producing a character vector with one element:

```{r}
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"), collapse = "|")

# Check length: The three output elements are collapsed into one element
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"), collapse = "|") %>% length()

# Check str_length: The collapsed result contains 5 characters
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"), collapse = "|") %>% str_length()
```

<br> **Example**: Using `str_c()` on more than one vector

When we provide multiple input vectors, `str_c()` joins them element by element: the first elements are joined together, the second elements are joined together, and so on.

```{r}
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"), c("x", "y", "z"), c("!", "?", ";"))
```

The default separator for each element-by-element combination is an empty character value (`""`), but we can customize it using the `sep` argument:

```{r}
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"), c("x", "y", "z"), c("!", "?", ";"), sep = "~")

# Check length: Output vector is same length as input vectors
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"), c("x", "y", "z"), c("!", "?", ";"), sep = "~") %>% length()
```

Again, we can use `collapse` to join the elements of the output vector into one element:

```{r}
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"), c("x", "y", "z"), c("!", "?", ";"), collapse = "|")

# Check length: The three output elements are collapsed into one element
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"), c("x", "y", "z"), c("!", "?", ";"), collapse = "|") %>% length()

# Specifying both `sep` and `collapse`
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"), c("x", "y", "z"), c("!", "?", ";"), sep = "~", collapse = "|")
```

<br> **Example**: Using `str_c()` on one-element character vectors

Each input below is a character vector containing one element:

Because `str_c()` joins corresponding elements, these three inputs are joined into one output element:

```{r}
str_c("a", "b", "c")

# These are explicitly written as one-element character vectors
str_c(c("a"), c("b"), c("c"))
```

We can use `sep` to specify how the elements are separated:

```{r}
str_c("a", "b", "c", sep = "~")
```

Because each input has one element, the output also has one element. Therefore, `collapse` has no effect here: there are not multiple output elements to join together.

```{r}
str_c("a", "b", "c", collapse = "|")
```

<br>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Using `str_c()` on types other than character</summary>

When we provide a non-character vector (such as a numeric or logical vector), it will get coerced into a character vector:

```{r}
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"), c(1, 2, 3), c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE))

# Specifying both `sep` and `collapse`
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"), c(1, 2, 3), c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE), sep = "~", collapse = "|")
```

We can also use single-element inputs of other types that can be coerced to character:

```{r}
str_c(TRUE, 1.5, 2L, "X") 
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Using `str_c()` on vectors of different lengths</summary>

<br> 

When trying to join vectors of different length, you will run into an error. 

-   This is because new recycling rules are applied to the `stringr` package to be consistent with other tidyverse recycling rules (see Wickham blog 12/05/2022)[https://www.tidyverse.org/blog/2022/12/stringr-1-5-0/#recycling-rules]

-   In practice this makes sense when working with data frames and tidyverse because columns (variables) in a data frame must be the same length. 


```{r, warning = FALSE, eval=FALSE}
str_c("#", c("a", "b", "c", "d"), c(1, 2, 3), c(TRUE, FALSE))

# Specifying both `sep` and `collapse`
str_c("#", c("a", "b", "c", "d"), c(1, 2, 3), c(TRUE, FALSE), sep = "~", collapse = "|")
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Using `str_c()` on dataframe columns</summary>

<br> 

Let's combine the `user_id` and `screen_name` columns from `p12_df`. We'll focus on unique Twitter handles:

```{r}
p12_unique_df <- p12_df %>% select(user_id, screen_name) %>% unique()
p12_unique_df
```

<br> **\[Base R method\]** Use `str_c()` to combine `user_id` and `screen_name`:

```{r}
str_c(p12_unique_df$user_id, "=", p12_unique_df$screen_name, sep = " ", collapse = ", ")
str_c(p12_unique_df$user_id, "=", p12_unique_df$screen_name, sep = " ") # without collapsing to one element
```

<br> **\[Tidyverse method\]** Use `str_c()` to combine `user_id` and `screen_name`:

```{r}
p12_unique_df %>% mutate(twitter_handle = str_c(user_id,screen_name))

p12_unique_df %>% mutate(twitter_handle = str_c("User #", user_id, " is @", screen_name))
```

</details>

## `str_sub()`

<br> **The `str_sub()` function**:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
?str_sub

# SYNTAX AND DEFAULT VALUES
str_sub(string = vec_name, start = 1L, end = -1L)
str_sub(vec_name, start = 1L, end = -1L, omit_na = FALSE) <- replacement_value
```

-   Function: Extract or replace parts of character values
-   Arguments:
    -   `string`: Character vector (or vector coercible to character)
    -   `start`: Position of first character to be included in substring (default: `1`)
    -   `end`: Position of last character to be included in substring (default: `-1`)
        -   A negative index means counting backward from the end of each character value
        -   If an element in the vector is shorter than the specified `end`, it will just include all the available characters that it does have
    -   `omit_na`: If `TRUE`, missing values in any of the arguments provided will result in an unchanged input
-   When `str_sub()` is used in the assignment form, you can replace the selected part of each character value with a `value` of your choice
    -   If an element in the vector is too short to meet the subset specification, the replacement `value` will be concatenated to the end of that element
    -   Note that this modifies your input vector directly, so you must have the vector saved to a variable (see example below)

<br>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Using `str_sub()` to extract parts of character values</summary>

<br> 

If no `start` and `end` positions are specified, `str_sub()` returns each complete input value by default:

```{r}
str_sub(string = c("abcdefg", 123, TRUE))
```

Note that if an element is shorter than the specified `end` (i.e., `123` in the example below), it will just include all the available characters that it does have:

```{r}
str_sub(string = c("abcdefg", 123, TRUE), start = 2, end = 4)
```

Remember we can also use negative index to count the position starting from the back:

```{r}
str_sub(string = c("abcdefg", 123, TRUE), start = 2, end = -2)
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Using `str_sub()` to replace parts of character values</summary>

<br> 

If no `start` and `end` positions are specified, `str_sub()` returns each complete input value by default, so the entire value would be replaced:

```{r}
vec_x <- c("A", "AB", "ABC", "ABCD", "ABCDE")
str_sub(string = vec_x, start = 1, end = -1)

str_sub(vec_x, start = 1, end = -1) <- "*"
vec_x
```

If an element in the vector is too short to meet the subset specification, the replacement `value` will be concatenated to the end of that element:

```{r}
vec_x <- c("A", "AB", "ABC", "ABCD", "ABCDE")
vec_x
str_sub(string = vec_x, start = 2, end = 3)

str_sub(vec_x, start = 2, end = 3) <- "*"
vec_x
```

Note that because the replacement form of `str_sub()` modifies the input vector directly, we need to save it in a variable first. Directly passing in the vector to `str_sub()` would give us an error:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Does not work
str_sub(c("A", "AB", "ABC", "ABCD", "ABCDE")) <- "*"
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Using `str_sub()` on dataframe column</summary>

<br> 

We can use `as.character()` to convert the `created_at` values to character data, then use `str_sub()` to extract various date/time components:

```{r}

#str(object = p12_df %>% select(created_at))
typeof(x = p12_df$created_at)
class(x = p12_df$created_at)
head(x = p12_df$created_at)

p12_datetime_df <- p12_df %>% select(created_at) %>%
  mutate(
      dt_chr = as.character(x = created_at), #convert to character
      date_chr = str_sub(string = dt_chr, start = 1, end = 10), #subset values in position 1 and 10 to grab the date
      yr_chr = str_sub(string = dt_chr, start = 1, end = 4), #subset values in position 1 and 4 to grab the year
      mth_chr = str_sub(string = dt_chr, start = 6, end = 7),
      day_chr = str_sub(string = dt_chr, start = 9, end = 10),
      hr_chr = str_sub(string = dt_chr, start = -8, end = -7),
      min_chr = str_sub(string = dt_chr, start = -5, end = -4),
      sec_chr = str_sub(string = dt_chr, start = -2, end = -1)
    )
p12_datetime_df
```

</details>

## Other `stringr` functions

Other useful `stringr` functions:

-   `str_to_upper()`: Turn character values to uppercase
-   `str_to_lower()`: Turn character values to lowercase
-   `str_sort()`: Sort a character vector
-   `str_trim()`: Trim whitespace from character values (including `\n`, `\t`, etc.)
-   `str_pad()`: Pad character values with a specified character

<br>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Using `str_to_upper()` to turn character values to uppercase</summary>

<br> 

Turn column names of `p12_df` to uppercase:

```{r}
# Column names are originally lowercase
names(x = p12_df)

# Turn column names to uppercase
names(p12_df) <- str_to_upper(string = names(x = p12_df))
names(x = p12_df)
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Using `str_to_lower()` to turn character values to lowercase</summary>

<br> 

Turn column names of `p12_df` to lowercase:

```{r}
# Column names are originally uppercase
names(x = p12_df)

# Turn column names to lowercase
names(p12_df) <- str_to_lower(string = names(x = p12_df))
names(x = p12_df)
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Using `str_sort()` to sort character vector</summary>

<br> 

Sort the vector of `p12_df` column names:

```{r}
# Before sort
names(x = p12_df)

# Sort alphabetically (default)
str_sort(x = names(x = p12_df))

# Sort reverse alphabetically
str_sort(x = names(x = p12_df), decreasing = TRUE)
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Using `str_trim()` to trim whitespace from character values</summary>

<br> 

```{r}
# Trim whitespace from both left and right sides (default)
str_trim(string = c("\nABC ", " XYZ\t"))

# Trim whitespace from left side
str_trim(string = c("\nABC ", " XYZ\t"), side = "left")

# Trim whitespace from right side
str_trim(string = c("\nABC ", " XYZ\t"), side = "right")
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Using `str_pad()` to pad character values</summary>

<br> 

Let's say we have a vector of zip codes that has lost all leading 0's. We can use `str_pad()` to add that back in:

```{r}
# Pad the left side of each character value with "0" until a width of 5 is reached
str_pad(string = c(95035, 90024, 5009, 5030), width = 5, side = "left", pad = "0")
```

</details>

# Dates and times

> "Date-time data can be frustrating to work with in R. R commands for date-times are generally unintuitive and change depending on the type of date-time object being used. Moreover, the methods we use with date-times must be robust to time zones, leap days, daylight savings times, and other time related quirks, and R lacks these capabilities in some situations. Lubridate makes it easier to do the things R does with date-times and possible to do the things R does not."

*Credit: `lubridate`[documentation](https://lubridate.tidyverse.org/)*

**How are dates and times stored in R?** (From [Dates and Times in R](https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~s133/dates.html))

-   The `Date` class is used for storing dates
    -   "Internally, `Date` objects are stored as the number of days since January 1, 1970, using negative numbers for earlier dates. The `as.numeric()` function can be used to convert a `Date` object to its internal form."
-   POSIX classes can be used for storing date plus times
    -   "The `POSIXct` class stores date/time values as the number of seconds since January 1, 1970"
    -   "The `POSIXlt` class stores date/time values as a list of components (hour, min, sec, mon, etc.) making it easy to extract these parts"
-   There is no native R class for storing only time

**Why use date/time objects?**

-   Using date/time objects makes it easier to fetch or modify various date/time components (e.g., year, month, day, day of the week)
    -   If the date/time is stored as character data, these components are not as readily accessible and must first be parsed
-   You can perform certain arithmetics with date/time objects (e.g., find the "difference" between date/time points)

## Creating date/time objects by parsing input

**Parse** means to read and interpret data according to a particular structure.

Functions that create date/time objects **by parsing character or numeric input**:

-   Create `Date` object: `ymd()`, `ydm()`, `mdy()`, `myd()`, `dmy()`, and `dym()`
    -   `y` stands for year, `m` stands for month, `d` stands for day
    -   Select the function that represents the order in which your date input is formatted, and the function will be able to parse your input and create a `Date` object
-   Create `POSIXct` object: `ymd_h()`, `ymd_hm()`, `ymd_hms()`, etc.
    -   `h` stands for hour, `m` stands for minute, `s` stands for second
    -   For any of the previous 6 date functions, you can append `h`, `hm`, or `hms` if you want to provide additional time information in order to create a `POSIXct` object
    -   To force a `POSIXct` object without providing any time information, you can just provide a timezone (using `tz`) to one of the date functions and it will assume midnight as the time
    -   You can use `Sys.timezone()` to get the timezone for your location

<br>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Creating `Date` object from character or numeric input</summary>

The `lubridate` functions are flexible and can parse dates in various formats:

```{r}
vec_x <- mdy("1/1/2024")
vec_x

vec_x <- mdy("1-1-2024")
vec_x

vec_x <- mdy("Jan. 1, 2024")
vec_x

vec_x <- ymd(20240101)
vec_x
```

<br> Investigate the `Date` object:

```{r}
class(x = vec_x)
typeof(x = vec_x)

# Number of days since January 1, 1970
as.numeric(x = vec_x)
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Creating `Date` objects from dataframe column</summary>

Using the `p12_datetime_df` we created earlier, we can create `Date` objects from the `date_chr` column:

```{r}
# Use `ymd()` to parse the character data stored in the `date_chr` column
p12_datetime_df %>% select(created_at, dt_chr, date_chr) %>%
  mutate(date_ymd = ymd(date_chr))
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Creating `POSIXct` object from character or numeric input</summary>

The `lubridate` functions are flexible and can parse AM/PM in various formats:

```{r}
vec_x <- mdy_h("12/31/2023 11pm")
vec_x

vec_x <- mdy_hm("12/31/2023 11:59 pm")
vec_x

vec_x <- mdy_hms("12/31/2023 11:59:59 PM")
vec_x

vec_x <- ymd_hms(20231231235959)
vec_x
```

<br> Investigate the `POSIXct` object:

```{r}
class(x = vec_x)
typeof(x = vec_x)

# Number of seconds since January 1, 1970
as.numeric(x = vec_x)
```

<br> We can also create a `POSIXct` object from a date function by providing a timezone. The time would default to midnight:

```{r}
vec_x <- mdy("1/1/2024", tz = "UTC")
vec_x

# Number of seconds since January 1, 1970
as.numeric(x = vec_x)  # Note that this is indeed 1 sec after the previous example
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Creating `POSIXct` objects from dataframe column</summary>

Using the `p12_datetime_df` we created earlier, we can recreate the `created_at` column (class `POSIXct`) from the `dt_chr` column (class `character`):

```{r}
# Use `ymd_hms()` to parse the character data stored in the `dt_chr` column
p12_datetime_df %>% select(created_at, dt_chr) %>%
  mutate(datetime_ymd_hms = ymd_hms(dt_chr))
```

</details>

## Creating date/time objects from individual components

Functions that create date/time objects **from various date/time components**:

-   Create `Date` object: `make_date()`
    -   Syntax and default values: `make_date(year = 1970L, month = 1L, day = 1L)`
    -   All inputs are coerced to integer
-   Create `POSIXct` object: `make_datetime()`
    -   Syntax and default values: `make_datetime(year = 1970L, month = 1L, day = 1L, hour = 0L, min = 0L, sec = 0, tz = "UTC")`
    - Input values should be numeric 

<br>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Creating `Date` object from individual components</summary>

There are various ways to pass in the inputs to create the same `Date` object:

```{r}
vec_x <- make_date(year = 2024, month = 1, day = 1)
vec_x

# Characters can be coerced to integers
vec_x <- make_date(year = "2024", month = "01", day = "01")
vec_x

# Remember that the default values for month and day would be 1L
vec_x <- make_date(year = 2024)
vec_x
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Creating `Date` objects from dataframe columns</summary>

Using the `p12_datetime_df` we created earlier, we can create `Date` objects from the various date component columns:

```{r}
# Use `make_date()` to create a `Date` object from the `yr_chr`, `mth_chr`, `day_chr` fields
p12_datetime_df %>% select(created_at, dt_chr, yr_chr, mth_chr, day_chr) %>%
  mutate(date_make_date = make_date(year = yr_chr, month = mth_chr, day = day_chr))
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Creating `POSIXct` object from individual components</summary>

```{r}
# Inputs should be numeric
vec_x <- make_datetime(
  year = 2023,
  month = 12,
  day = 31,
  hour = 23,
  min = 59,
  sec = 59
)
vec_x
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Creating `POSIXct` objects from dataframe columns</summary>

Using the `p12_datetime_df` we created earlier, we can recreate the `created_at` column (class `POSIXct`) from the various date and time component columns (class `character`):

```{r}
# Use `make_datetime()` to create a `POSIXct` object from the `yr_chr`, `mth_chr`, `day_chr`, `hr_chr`, `min_chr`, `sec_chr` fields
# Convert inputs to integers first
p12_datetime_df %>%
  mutate(datetime_make_datetime = make_datetime(
    year = as.integer(x = yr_chr),
    month = as.integer(x = mth_chr),
    day = as.integer(x = day_chr),
    hour = as.integer(x = hr_chr),
    min = as.integer(x = min_chr),
    sec = as.integer(x = sec_chr)
  )) %>%
  select(datetime_make_datetime, yr_chr, mth_chr, day_chr, hr_chr, min_chr, sec_chr)
```

</details>

## Date/time object components

Storing data using date/time objects makes it easier to **get and set** the various date/time components.

-   Basic accessor functions:
    -   `date()`: Date component
    -   `year()`: Year
    -   `month()`: Month
    -   `day()`: Day
    -   `hour()`: Hour
    -   `minute()`: Minute
    -   `second()`: Second
    -   `week()`: Week of the year
    -   `wday()`: Day of the week (`1` for Sunday to `7` for Saturday)
    -   `am()`: Is it in the am? (returns `TRUE` or `FALSE`)
    -   `pm()`: Is it in the pm? (returns `TRUE` or `FALSE`)
-   To **get** a date/time component, you can simply pass a date/time object to the function
    -   Syntax: `accessor_function(x = date_time_object)`
-   To **set** a date/time component, you can assign into the accessor function to change the component
    -   Syntax: `accessor_function(date_time_object) <- new_component`
    -   Note that `am()` and `pm()` can't be set. Modify the time components instead.

<br>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Getting date/time components</summary>

```{r}
# Create datetime for New Year's Eve
vec_x <- make_datetime(
  year = 2023,
  month = 12,
  day = 31,
  hour = 23,
  min = 59,
  sec = 59
)
vec_x
vec_x %>% class()

# Get date
date(x = vec_x)

# Get hour
hour(x = vec_x)

# Is it pm?
pm(x = vec_x)

# Day of the week (1 = Sunday)
wday(x = vec_x)

year(x = vec_x)
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Setting date/time components</summary>

```{r}
# Create datetime for New Year's Eve
vec_x <- make_datetime(
  year = 2023,
  month = 12,
  day = 31,
  hour = 23,
  min = 59,
  sec = 59
)
vec_x

# Get week of year
week(x = vec_x)

# Set week of year (move back 1 week)
week(vec_x) <- week(x = vec_x) - 1

# Date now moved from New Year's Eve to Christmas Eve
vec_x

# Set day to Christmas Day
day(vec_x) <- 25

# Date now moved from Christmas Eve to Christmas Day
vec_x
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Getting date/time components from dataframe column</summary>

Using the `p12_datetime_df` we created earlier, we can isolate the various date/time components from the `POSIXct` object in the `created_at` column:

```{r}
# The extracted date/time components will be of numeric type
p12_datetime_df %>% select(created_at) %>%
  mutate(
    yr_num = year(x = created_at),
    mth_num = month(x = created_at),
    day_num = day(x = created_at),
    hr_num = hour(x = created_at),
    min_num = minute(x = created_at),
    sec_num = second(x = created_at),
    ampm = ifelse(
      test = am(x = created_at),
      yes = 'AM',
      no = 'PM'
    )  # am()/pm() returns TRUE/FALSE
  )
```

</details>

## Time spans

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anyone-can-cook/rclass2/master/assets/images/time_spans.png)

3 ways to represent time spans (From [lubridate cheatsheet](https://rawgit.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/master/lubridate.pdf))

-   **Intervals** represent specific intervals of the timeline, bounded by start and end date-times
    -   Example: People with birthdays between the **interval** October 23 to November 22 are Scorpios
-   **Periods** track changes in clock times, which ignore time line irregularities
    -   Example: Daylight savings time ends at the beginning of November and we gain an hour - this extra hour is *ignored* when determining the **period** between October 23 to November 22
-   **Durations** track the passage of physical time, which deviates from clock time when irregularities occur
    -   Example: Daylight savings time ends at the beginning of November and we gain an hour - this extra hour is *added* when determining the **duration** between October 23 to November 22

**Time spans using `lubridate`**

Using the `lubridate` package for time spans:

-   **Interval**
    -   Create an interval using `interval()` or `%--%`
        -   Syntax: `interval(start = start_datetime, end = end_datetime)` or `start_datetime %--% end_datetime`
-   **Periods**
    -   "Periods are time spans but don’t have a fixed length in seconds, instead they work with '*human*' times, like days and months." (From [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/dates-and-times.html#periods))
    -   Create periods using functions whose name is the time unit pluralized (e.g., `years()`, `months()`, `weeks()`, `days()`, `hours()`, `minutes()`, `seconds()`)
        -   Example: `days(x = 1)` creates a period of 1 day - it does not matter if this day happened to have an extra hour due to daylight savings ending, since periods do not have a physical length

            ```{r}
            days(x = 1)
            ```
    -   You can add and subtract periods
    -   You can also use `as.period()` to get period of an interval
-   **Durations**
    -   Durations keep track of the physical amount of time elapsed, so it is "stored as seconds, the only time unit with a consistent length" (From [lubridate cheatsheet](https://rawgit.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/master/lubridate.pdf))
    -   Create durations using functions whose name is the time unit prefixed with a `d` (e.g., `dyears()`, `dweeks()`, `ddays()`, `dhours()`, `dminutes()`, `dseconds()`)
        -   Example: `ddays(x = 1)` creates a duration of `86400s`, using the standard conversion of `60` seconds in an minute, `60` minutes in an hour, and `24` hours in a day:

            ```{r}
            ddays(x = 1)
            ```

            Notice that the output says this is equivalent to *approximately* `1` day, since it acknowledges that not all days have `24` hours. In the case of daylight savings, one particular day may have `25` hours, so the duration of that day should be represented as:

            ```{r}
            ddays(x = 1) + dhours(x = 1)
            ```
    -   You can add and subract durations
    -   You can also use `as.duration()` to get duration of an interval

<br>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Working with interval</summary>

```{r}
# Use `Sys.timezone()` to get timezone for your location (time is midnight by default)
scorpio_start <- ymd("2023-10-23", tz = Sys.timezone())
scorpio_end <- ymd("2023-11-22", tz = Sys.timezone())

scorpio_start
# These datetime objects have class `POSIXct`
class(x = scorpio_start)

# Create interval for the datetimes
scorpio_interval <- scorpio_start %--% scorpio_end  # or `interval(start = scorpio_start, end = scorpio_end)`
scorpio_interval <- interval(start = scorpio_start, end = scorpio_end)
scorpio_interval

# The object has class `Interval`
class(x = scorpio_interval)
as.numeric(x = scorpio_interval)
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Working with period</summary>

If we use `as.period()` to get the period of `scorpio_interval`, we see that it is a period of `30` days. We do not worry about the extra `1` hour gained due to daylight savings ending:

```{r}
# Period is 30 days
scorpio_period <- as.period(x = scorpio_interval)
scorpio_period

# The object has class `Period`
class(x = scorpio_period)
```

<br> Because periods work with "human" times like days, it is more intuitive. For example, if we add a period of `30` days to the `scorpio_start` datetime object, we get the expected end datetime that is `30` days later:

```{r}
# Start datetime for Scorpio birthdays (time is midnight)
scorpio_start

# After adding 30 day period, we get the expected end datetime (time is midnight)
scorpio_start + days(x = 30)
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Working with duration</summary>

If we use `as.duration()` to get the duration of `scorpio_interval`, we see that it is a duration of `2595600` seconds. It takes into account the extra `1` hour gained due to daylight savings ending:

```{r}
# Duration is 2595600 seconds, which is equivalent to 30 24-hr days + 1 additional hour
scorpio_duration <- as.duration(x = scorpio_interval)
scorpio_duration

# The object has class `Duration`
class(x = scorpio_duration)

# Using the standard 60s/min, 60min/hr, 24hr/day conversion,
# confirm duration is slightly more than 30 "standard" (ie. 24-hr) days
2595600 / (60 * 60 * 24)

# Specifically, it is 30 days + 1 hour, if we define a day to have 24 hours
seconds_to_period(x = scorpio_duration)
```

<br> Because durations work with physical time, when we add a duration of `30` days to the `scorpio_start` datetime object, we do not get the end datetime we'd expect:

```{r}
# Start datetime for Scorpio birthdays (time is midnight)
scorpio_start

# After adding 30 day duration, we do not get the expected end datetime
# `ddays(x = 30)` adds the number of seconds in 30 standard 24-hr days, but one of the days has 25 hours
scorpio_start + ddays(x = 30)

# We need to add the additional 1 hour of physical time that elapsed during this time span
scorpio_start + ddays(x = 30) + dhours(x = 1)
```

</details>

<br>

# Appendix

## Special Characters

An **escape sequence** starts with a backslash (`\`) and allows us to include characters that would otherwise have a special meaning in character data.

*Credit: [Escape sequences](https://campus.datacamp.com/courses/string-manipulation-with-stringr-in-r/string-basics?ex=4) from DataCamp*

<br> **Special characters** are characters that will not be interpreted literally.

Common **special characters**:

-   `\n`: newline
-   `\t`: tab
-   `\`: used for escaping purposes
    -   `\'`: literal single quote
    -   `\"`: literal double quote
    -   `\\`: literal backslash

A backslash gives the character that follows it a special meaning. For example, `n` by itself is the ordinary letter `n`, while `\n` represents a newline.

<br> **The `writeLines()` function**:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
?writeLines

# SYNTAX AND DEFAULT VALUES
writeLines(text = vec_name, con = stdout(), sep = "\n", useBytes = FALSE)
```

-   "`writeLines()` displays quotes and backslashes as they would be read, rather than as R stores them." (From [writeLines](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/base/versions/3.6.2/topics/writeLines) documentation)
-   When character data include **escape sequences**, `writeLines()` helps us see how the text will be interpreted
-   `writeLines()` also displays the text without the outer pair of double quotes, so we see only the content of each character value

<br>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Escaping single quotes</summary>

```{r}
vec_x <- 'Escaping single quote \' within single quotes'
vec_x
```

Alternatively, we could have created the character value using double quotes:

```{r}
vec_x <- "Single quote ' within double quotes does not need escaping"
vec_x
```

Using `writeLines()` shows only the content of the character value, without the outer pair of double quotes:

```{r}
writeLines(text = vec_x)
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Escaping double quotes</summary>

```{r}
vec_x <- "Escaping double quote \" within double quotes"
vec_x
```

Alternatively, we could have created the character value using single quotes:

```{r}
vec_x <- 'Double quote " within single quotes does not need escaping'
vec_x
```

Notice how the backslash still appeared in the output because R needed to distinguish the inner double quote from the outer pair of double quotes. `writeLines()` displays only the text as it will be interpreted:

```{r}
writeLines(text = vec_x)
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Escaping double quotes within double quotes</summary>

```{r}
vec_x <- "I called my mom and she said \"Echale ganas!\""
vec_x
```

Using `writeLines()` shows the character value as interpreted, without displaying the backslashes:

```{r}
writeLines(text = vec_x)
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Escaping backslashes</summary>

To include a literal backslash in character data, we need to escape the backslash with another backslash:

```{r}
vec_x <- "The executable is located in C:\\Program Files\\Git\\bin"
vec_x
```

Use `writeLines()` to see how the character value is interpreted:

```{r}
writeLines(text = vec_x)
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Other special characters</summary>

```{r}
vec_x <- "A\tB\nC\tD"
vec_x
```

Use `writeLines()` to see how the character value is interpreted:

```{r}
writeLines(text = vec_x)
```

</details>

**Escape special characters using Twitter data**

Let's take a look at some tweets from our PAC-12 universities.

-   Let's start by grabbing observations 1-3 from the `text` column.

```{r}
#Twitter example of \n newline special characters
p12_df$text[1:3]
```

-   Using `writeLines()` we can see the character values as they would be read, rather than as R stores them.

```{r}
writeLines(text = p12_df$text[1:3])
```

<details>

<summary>**Example**: Escaping double quotes using Twitter data</summary>

-   Twitter data may contain many character values with double quotes.

    -   In the example below, the character value includes `\"` and `\n` to escape the double quotes and represent a newline.

    ```{r}
    #Twitter example of \" double quotes special characters
    p12_df$text[24]
    ```

-   Using `writeLines()` we can see the character values as they would be read, rather than as R stores them.

    -   We no longer see the escape sequences `\"` or `\n`

    ```{r}
    writeLines(text = p12_df$text[24])
    ```

</details>
